claim: What forced Nixon's resignation was the cover-up, captured on the "smoking gun" tape: a June 23, 1972 Oval Office conversation (six days after the break-in) in which Nixon approved a plan to have the CIA tell the FBI to halt its Watergate investigation on bogus national-security grounds — "have Walters call Pat Gray and just say, 'Stay the hell out of this.'" The Supreme Court ordered the tape's release in United States v. Nixon; it was made public August 5, 1974, his remaining congressional support collapsed, and Nixon resigned August 9, 1974. (Geoff Shepard, the junior Nixon lawyer who transcribed the tape, coined the phrase "smoking gun.") What Nixon "was guilty of was saying, cover it up."

sources.label: Watergate.info — transcript of the June 23, 1972 "smoking gun" tape (Nixon–Haldeman).
sources.quote: That the way to handle this now is for us to have Walters call Pat Gray and just say, “Stay the hell out of this…this is ah, business here we don’t want you to go any further on it.”

sources.label: Miller Center (UVA) — "Smoking Gun" tape and its role in the resignation.

notes: Group A. Same June 23, 1972 tape also contains Nixon's 'open the whole Bay of Pigs thing' line — the obstruction (this record) and the contested JFK-code reading (1972-bay-of-pigs-jfk-001) come from one conversation. Geoff Shepard (the reel's 'Jeff Shepard') is the former Nixon aide who transcribed it and coined 'smoking gun'; his books argue prosecutorial misconduct, and he detailed this on the Tucker Carlson Show (Aug 2024).
